utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon. I'm sorry that it was necessary to start a little late because the previous Chamber was delayed in completing their morning sitting. Good afternoon, Doctor, and once again, may I remind you of the affirmation that you took at the beginning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can Your Honours just excuse me for one moment. I'm looking for something. Thank you, Your Honours. Examined by Mr. Re: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon again, Dr. Ciganovic. Yesterday and the day before you were telling the Chamber about your experience in diagnosing explosive injuries when performing autopsies. How many bodies have you examined in which you have determined that an explosive injury contributed to the cause of death? And I obviously mean an estimate of how many bodies you have examined.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot recall the exact number, but the total number of persons killed in the war in the months referred to was a bit above 100. Between 100 and 150 people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in total?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in total, apart from those you examined during that part of the war?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Generally speaking, in my entire practice up to that date, as I've already said, I examined a total of about 8.000 cadavers, either personally or in consultation with my colleagues. And a part of these -- a certain number of these had died owing to explosive wounds, but I cannot recall the exact number.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you able to give an estimate?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, explosive wounds are less frequent in peacetime conditions, so that this number generally ranges around 1 per cent or under 1 per cent of all forensic autopsies in peacetime conditions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the procedure in 1991 in Dubrovnik in Croatia -- I'm sorry, in Dubrovnik for issuing death certificates following an autopsy?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After an autopsy was performed, in this period I would fill in and sign a death certificate, which was an official document which would later be transmitted to the registry which was located in the court building in Dubrovnik, and then the clerk of the registry would issue an application of death, would inscribe the dead person in the registry of deaths and would issue a licence for the funeral.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can the witness please be shown these two documents.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There are two documents. Can you -- just a moment. Turning to the first document, which is number 52 of 1992, dated the 16th of January, 1992, turning to Mr. Urban, what is that document?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an extract from the registry of deaths. This is a document which is issued by the registrar in the registry of the -- of Dubrovnik municipality and which actually confirms that a certain person has died.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, is that a death certificate relating to the death of Pavo Urban on the 6th of January -- sorry, 6th of December, 1991?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What role, if any, did you have in having that certificate prepared?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've already said, prior to this I would issue a confirmation of death or a death certificate, which was then followed by a notice of death which was issued by the registry and then also a death certificate or an extract from the death registry. Without my own document, which is a certificate of death, this other document could not be issued.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Secondly, could you turn to the other document in front of you, which is number 530 of 1992, dated the 18th of December, 1992. Can you please tell the Trial Chamber briefly what that document is.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the same type of document as the previous one, so that I have nothing to add.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And does this relate to the death of Mr. Skocko on the 6th of December, 1991?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is. By this document Skocko Tonci was officially declared dead.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And from your last answer are you telling the Trial Chamber that this death certificate would have been issued based upon the document that you prepared?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: May those two documents be received into evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: They will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: First document pertaining to 1992 will be Prosecution Exhibit P73, the second document, Prosecution Exhibit P74.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Ciganovic, you told the Trial Chamber at the beginning of your evidence that you left for Pancevo at the end of 1992. Why did you leave Dubrovnik for Pancevo?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I left for personal reasons. What I'm saying, that was -- that I was not forced to leave Dubrovnik, and I believe that my personal reasons are not of relevance to this court.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: That's the cross -- sorry, the Prosecution's examination-in-chief, Your Honours. I'll just say in relation to the two documents -- three documents which are in that file, I note the objection to their tender at the moment and obviously will deal with that later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Re. Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. And I ask the usher for the lectern, please. If he would be so kind as to bring it to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Your Honours, with leave, my learned colleague Ms. Comers has reminded me of a question which I neglected to ask of the doctor. Could I seek leave to reopen before my learned friend starts?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Could I ask you to pause a moment, Mr. Rodic. Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were giving some evidence about viewing Mr. Urban's body when it was brought to your hospital for the autopsy, and the report which you -- and you've looked at the report. Can you tell the Trial Chamber about any personal items Mr. Urban had with him or were near his body when it was brought to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When he was brought to hospital, apart from his clothing and his footwear, I cannot exactly remember, but I don't think that he had any other personal effects. I apologise. No. I just remembered. There was a camera, a still camera, and I believe that there was a bag for the camera, a photographic one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And some documents were also found on him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Ciganovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Cross-examined by Mr. Rodic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Ciganovic, good afternoon, I'm Defence counsel Goran Rodic, Defence counsel for Mr. Strugar, and I will be asking you some questions on his behalf. These questions will have to do with your testimony in this particular case. As we speak the same language, would you be so kind as to pause briefly after my questions so as to allow for the translation. Thank you. So you graduated from the medical school in Zagreb in 1973; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After that, you worked as a general practitioner in Dubrovnik until 1979?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From 1979 to 1983, you pursued and completed your specialised studies in pathology and cytology and obtained a master's degree in pathology?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I enrolled in post-graduate studies as well as obtained my master's degree in the field of pathology.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me whether cytology is a part of pathology.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the Croatian university, cytology is a special, separate specialised stream. These studies can be pursued separately or one can complete these studies by first completing specialised studies in pathology and then pursuing a post-graduate course in specifically cytology, whereby one acquires the degree of specialist in pathology.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you -- have you completed these studies as well?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the medical faculty in Zagreb, is it true that forensic medicine is a separate subject which is studied at the fifth year of studies while pathology is studied at the third year of faculty?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are the forensic medicine building and the pathology buildings at Salata in Zagreb separated?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is there a difference, a distinction between a forensic medicine specialist and a clinical pathology specialist?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true that a clinical pathologist is not a forensic pathologist, a forensic medicine specialist?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then it is the case that these are two different specialisation fields?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did there exist at that time a separate specialised study stream for forensic medicine in the former SFRY?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did this specialisation course last three years?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the university in Zagreb it lasted four years.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned during the examination-in-chief, inter alia, that over a certain period of time, you performed forensic medicine autopsies at the Forensic Medicine Institute in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true that Zagreb does not have a Forensic Medicine Institute?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It does have an institute. It is called the Forensic Medicine Institute, and the difference is only in name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It is called Institute for Forensic Medicine and the Crime of the Medical University in Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is its name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So your specialised studies were in the field of clinical pathology and not in the area of forensic medicine; right?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First I completed my specialised studies in clinical pathology and later I also pursued my studies and completed my studies in forensic medicine and cytology.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many diplomas do you have?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have three diplomas, specialised degrees.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From 1992 to 1996, did you work at the clinical centre in Belgrade in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From 1993, the second half of that year, I worked at the clinical centre until 1997.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you sought employment, did you provide evidence of all of these three specialisations of yours?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you work at the first surgical clinic?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you work at the gynecological clinic in that period?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While you were working in the clinical centre of Serbia what was your particular duty and job?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the clinical centre of Serbia, I worked as a clinical pathologist for the first surgical clinic, which is engaged in gastrointestinal surgery and also for the emergency centre as well as for the second surgical clinic which is specialised for cardiovascular and endocrinological pathology and that was my work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you performed autopsies there?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there I didn't perform any autopsies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true that autopsies are done at the Institute for Pathology there and if there is anything which is questionable then autopsies are undertaken at the Forensic Medicine Institute?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you affiliated to any party in that period?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I am not wrong, you said that you -- that after your first specialised studies you continued working in Dubrovnik. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you also said that you would occasionally depart for Zagreb, when you referred to the Institute for Forensic Medicine, that you would go there once a week. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How is it possible while pursuing -- pursuing four years of specialised studies on a part-time basis? That is not the customary situation, is it?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it isn't, but I have to explain. To pursue specialised pathological studies, which normally at the Zagreb university lasts four years and specialised studies in forensic medicine which normally also take four years, they have a common period of residency, which is a year and a half, so that a person specialising in either of these two subjects needs to pursue specialised studies in the other field for another two years and a half. So in my particular case, this extended to four years precisely because I was unable to be in Zagreb on a continuous basis to pursue all those studies because I was working at the same time also in Dubrovnik, as I've already explained.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was this not regular schooling, so to speak? Specialisation lasting four years actually necessitates the presence of the trainee.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, specialisation is not a part of regular education. It is a training course which also involves sitting for colloquia and at the end of the studies sitting for a specialised exam with mentors and professors in the particular branch of medicine. Mentors and professors in that particular branch conclude that the candidate is able to sit for such an exam, but not prior to the expiry of the prescribed time for such studies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When I said regular full-time education, what I had in mind is regular attendance during the four years of specialised studies. Isn't that common practice when pursuing a specialised course of studies?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is the established practice for most specialised courses except in cases like mine, which is by no means rare, where people had to continue working at the same time at their institution or in a clinic and study at the same time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was this in the best interests of the Health Ministry of Croatia to approve this course of studies for you and to make it possible for you Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. to attend part-time?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was in the best interest of the Health Ministry because there are not too many specials of that particular profile around. They are a bit thin on the ground. In Croatia, and even in Yugoslavia, there weren't too many of those around at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Currently you are working at the Pancevo hospital?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which specific position do you occupy there?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am the chief pathologist, cytologist, and chief of the department for forensic medicine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you also work for courts in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I also work for the various courts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you -- is your name on any of the lists of permanent court experts with any court in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, my name is there on the list of district court in Pancevo and that of the municipal court in Pancevo, the municipal court in Kovin, that in Kovacica, in Alibunar in Vrsac, in Bijela Crkva, in South Banat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is the procedure any different in terms of performing an autopsy at the Pancevo court in relation to the work you did in the Dubrovnik court?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there's no difference.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is everything done in more or less the same way pursuant to the Law on Criminal Procedure?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The job of a forensic expert is always done pursuant to -- in compliance with the Law on Criminal Procedure. The method used in performing an autopsy depends on the school you went to. There are various schools. There are certain small differences in terms of practice between the study and the application of forensic medicine in Zagreb and at the Belgrade institute respectively. Essentially the two are, however, the same.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the course of 1990 - I'm talking about the year 1990 - were you made to sign any documents expressing your loyalty to the Croatian authorities?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was never made to sign any documents like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were other people made to sign any such documents?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard that this was the case with some people, but I never witnessed anything like that myself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear that this was imposed on people as a condition for them to keep their jobs?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I heard about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With you at the Dubrovnik hospital at that time, were there also Vera Vukcevic-Rados, Dusanka Ljubibratic?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Back in 1992, were those two persons fired?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dusanka Ljubibratic, as far as I know, was transferred from the hospital to the children's health centre. I'm not sure if there was a period of time where she was out of job.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about the other person, Vera Vukcevic?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think Vera Vukcevic left Dubrovnik altogether, but we were not really close. So what I'm telling you now is based on what I heard.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there quite a number of doctors who were Serbs in Dubrovnik who left Dubrovnik during this period of time?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the Dubrovnik medical centre, there were a number of Serb doctors working there, but they were the minority if you look at the overall number of doctors working in the area. As far as I know, the majority of them stayed in Dubrovnik, and they still work there today. Some left Dubrovnik before the war, and I left after the war. This colleague of mine that we have just referred to, Vera Vukcevic, also.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The reason those people left their jobs was to move out of Dubrovnik. Was it because their working conditions were different before the war and after the war?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe the war affected their decision to leave. At least that was true of a number of these people. Not only the ones that we have referred to but also other people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the war affect your decision to leave also? Was there any pressure of any sorts?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not on me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not referring to you, I'm referring to the situation at work.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Personally, I faced no such pressure at work. No threats were ever made, no indication even that I might be out of a job soon, or any pressure in my private life, for that matter. The status I enjoyed in Dubrovnik was very good, in other words.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what made you leave? You had worked at Dubrovnik hospital for a long time, after all, and you were the only pathologist of that particular type there.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My wife and my five-year-old soon left Dubrovnik during the war when the first convoys or, rather, ships started leaving Dubrovnik. As my wife had grown up in Pancevo, she has relatives there and she owns a flat in Pancevo. So first she left for Split, then she went to Sarajevo, and finally she ended up in Pancevo. She remained there until my arrival. I opposed her return to Dubrovnik, her early return to Dubrovnik, and that's why she remained without a job back in Dubrovnik. She was a teacher, and my son started going to school in Pancevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, did any of your relatives remain in Dubrovnik? Is there still anyone living there?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After I left Dubrovnik, my parents stayed behind in our family house in Dubrovnik. My father died a year later, and my mother still lives there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is a family home, your family home outside the walls of the Old Town, as far as I understand.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the flat in the Old Town, that also belongs to you, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it doesn't belong to us because my grandfather had died in the meantime, and he was married two times, so his widow inherited that flat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We'll go back to that later, but please tell me about the following terms: "Autopsy" and "post-mortem" mean the same thing, don't they?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me exactly what "full autopsy" means, what the term implies.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Full autopsy is carried out according to the following procedure: First there is an external examination of the body, after which you open parts of the body; the head, the thorax, the abdomen. All the internal organs are extracted, taken out, and facts are established.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true then that the written report contains the introduction, the finding -- the findings of the external examination, the findings of the internal examination, and death established?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you use Zecevic's, Milovanovic's or Pejakovic's textbooks during your studies?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I used those manuals, especially Zecevic's book. Zecevic was from the Forensic Medicine Institute in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All these three names are familiar to you?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These names, were these people the founders of forensic medicine, as it were, in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They were not the founders.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Or, rather, they were among the most renowned experts in the field?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were famous experts in the field, but the Forensic Medicine Institute in Belgrade and the institute in Zagreb had been founded long before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true, then -- is it true that when looking at a forensic medical finding, if you were to establish cause of death, you would need to conduct a full autopsy for such a finding to be accurate?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That is not true. It is not always necessary to carry out full autopsy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you learn that?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the Forensic Medicine Institute in Zagreb. As far as I know, the same thing is taught at the Forensic Medicine Institute in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I underlined "forensic medical finding." Is it your submission that without a full autopsy being carried out, you can stand up in court and defend your findings on the cause of death?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is indeed my submission.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Based on what?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a court expert, I have been trained to identify the signs and symptoms of bodily injuries, their results, and the physiology of what goes on in the human body between the time harm is inflicted and the time death occurs. It was very often the case in my career that I took the stand as an expert and testified as to the cause of death, even when no autopsy had been performed, or sometimes based on autopsies that had been conducted by other people who were also forensic pathologists. Taking into account the symptoms, the therapy that a patient had been prescribed, all the signs that had been apparent until the time of death and everything that was established later, I would often be called to present my conclusions and determine cause of death. This procedure is very often applied when death is caused by traffic accidents, in order to establish a link between a specific traffic accident and death. This is much easier to do if there is -- if there is an autopsy that is conducted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: By definition, an autopsy implies that cavities are opened, body cavities are opened.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does indeed imply that. If you look at the contemporary literature on the subject, there are different ways to perform an autopsy on a human body. According to some authorities, an autopsy is conducted by opening the cavities and inspecting the organs on the spot without actually extracting the organs from the body. According to the Zagreb and Belgrade schools, all internal organs must be taken out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us try to simplify matters and make this perfectly understandable for laymen. You said that based on medical documents, you are able to establish the cause of death; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in some cases.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you perform an autopsy in all the cases, is it possible for you to accurately establish the cause of death as a rule?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not as a rule.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, but the likelihood of an accurate diagnosis would be much higher, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you perform an autopsy, you can find out a lot of information, and you can trace some changes in the body that may help you to determine the cause of death. However, if death is not instantaneous following the injury, if there was some form of treatment in the meantime, then it is necessary to be familiar with all the facts, all the symptoms, and everything that was done between the injury and the time that death occurred for you to reach an accurate conclusion. In cases like these, forensic autopsy -- performing an autopsy is not sufficient evidence for you to be able to establish the cause of death accurately.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You make a link between the time the injury occurred and the time death occurs. Death can be instantaneous, death can occur two days later or two months later after the original injury. So you say you need to look at the documents of what went on in the meantime between the injury and the death in order for you to be able to establish the cause of death.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is what I'm saying.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That wasn't my question. When I said an autopsy, I also include both an instantaneous death and a later death in relation to the original injury. What I'm asking is, forensically speaking, is that the only reliable criterion to establish the cause of death?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Performing an autopsy is certainly the most reliable way to determine the cause of death.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The external examination, or findings following an external examination, as some people call it, this is only part of the entire job of performing an autopsy?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you perform an external examination, you cannot accurately establish the cause of death, medically speaking and forensically speaking?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In forensic and medical terms, whenever an external examination is conducted, it must be ordered by the court --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, but that's not what I'm asking you. It is precisely due to the nature of our subject that I'm trying to get you to provide answers that are as brief as possible. What I was saying is that an external examination is not sufficient to accurately establish the cause of death. Am I right in claiming that?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: An external -- an external examination in some cases may be sufficient to accurately establish the cause of death.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What are these specific cases?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm talking about cases like the ones under discussion here where one faces severe injuries with clear signs of haemorrhage.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Severe injuries, extensive injuries, what does that mean; one individual injury, five different injuries, ten injuries, 20 injuries, or perhaps body parts lying scattered all the over the place? Is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you have body parts that were scattered and then you collect them, in these cases it is very difficult to determine the cause of death. It's much easier to determine the cause of death if you have only one or several injuries. In these cases, we were looking at bodies which had sustained one or several injuries. The vital reactions were clear, and signs of haemorrhage were clear.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please let us try not to waste time. I'm afraid I'll have to ask this in a very graphic manner. If after you body which shows one injury one centimetre across, for example, if you perform an external examination of the body, in forensic terms and medical terms, can you establish accurately the cause of death?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, you can't, and that's when one has to perform a partial autopsy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We'll get to that -- we'll get to that in due course. Is it correct that more often than not, with the possible exception of very extreme cases, more often than not an external examination is used to make an assumption on what the cause of death may be? Is this not the case? I keep speaking in forensic terms and in medical terms.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and when I make an assumption, I perform a partial or full autopsy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So we agree that the most reliable thing to establish the cause of death is a complete post-mortem examination?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To ascertain, establish all bodily injuries, if they are the cause of death, that is the most reliable.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you, in your practice of your work before courts have provided them your written findings and opinions, can you express in percentage terms what you have done before courts as an expert? Namely, when you defend your findings before court, do you do it on the basis of a complete post-mortem examination or do you defend your findings as to the cause of death on the basis of an external examination only? If that is the case, please indicate what court and what particular cases or examples this was.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 3 to 5 per cent of the cases, it is the court which orders, following my own recommendation, that only an external examination of the cadaver be undertaken in order for the cause of death to be established. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. That is, of course, the case in obvious instances where a complete autopsy is not required.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it is just in 3 to 5 per cent of the cases, and only if you make this recommendation the examining magistrate can approve an external examination of the corpse; right?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Not even in these cases is the examining magistrate under the obligation to accept your recommendation but may order a complete autopsy?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you give me, in connection with this 3 to 5 per cent number, can you give me an indication of these obvious cases? What is an obvious case?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: An obvious case is, for instance, a case of severe bodily injury when injuries were inflicted by large calibre firearms, for instance a hunting carbine, a hunting rifle, from close range, or accidents sustained at work where there was extensive bodily harm but with clear signs of how death occurred. For instance, if a machine compressed a person's head at work, a complete post-mortem examination needs to be undertaken because he could have dropped it before his head fell into the machine. But if the machine tore off his arm and he bled to death, then that is a clear cause of death.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you right away at this point. After the machine tore off his arm and he bled to death, you say that that is a clear cause of death. And this is what you would establish by an external examination or external finding or, rather, you could provide your opinion as to that being the cause of death; is that so? And what I am asking you is from the moment the machine cut off his arm up to the moment when you think he bled to death, could he have had a heart attack and died of it? Just tell me briefly yes or no.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you assert that?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Death because of cardiac arrest is because of the arrest of work of the heart, but if cardiac arrest occurred before a person bled to death I would not find the signs of total blood loss on the cadaver -- on the corpse.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does the term "anemia" mean anything to you; and what does it mean?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Anemia" means reduced number of red blood cells relative to the average number in the laboratory tests.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's try to sail through this question more easily. So from the moment the machine cut off the hand of -- the arm of the person and the moment to this total blood loss, can perhaps this person have sustained brain stroke and died of brain stroke?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The answer is the same as in the case of cardiac arrest.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then can you establish by external examination, can you assist on that basis from the moment the arm was cut off what the intensity of the bleeding was, what the time required until death occurred was? Can you state that clearly? Can you provide a clear answer to these questions, and was perhaps cardiac -- a heart stroke, perhaps a heart stroke occur in the meantime? Can you answer all these questions clearly on the basis of an external examination, and can you claim that always in the -- in the forensic medical sense?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the moment the arm was cut off to the death of that particular person due to haemorrhage, the duration of that time is individual. It varies from individual to individual. It can take from three to four minutes up to ten minutes after the injury was sustained without the administration of any sort of treatment. In order for total haemorrhage to occur, total blood loss to occur, the mechanism is as follows: The heart pumps out through open blood vessels, pumps the blood outside, and when the blood vessels have been almost completely evacuated, death occurs. In order for me to establish terminal haemorrhage, external examination does not only imply visible inspection, it also implies dissecting a section of the tissue, of the skin, and of the deep blood vessels in order for me to be able to ascertain the quantity of blood which remains in the body.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you cannot ascertain that by an external examination; is that so?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do that during my external examination.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: External examination, mind you, so nothing partial, two-thirds. We know exactly what an external examination means.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: External examination implies all these things. Of course, a partial autopsy is quite something different, and a complete post-mortem examination yet a third thing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm asking about the external examination.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I suspect total blood loss, I apply external examination and other methods if I'm able to, like pathohistological methods.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As we are in the juristic field, may I kindly ask you -- of course I can ask you specific questions for all these various procedures, but when you say only external examination without all these other partial procedures and so on, we have the external finding, the internal finding. I'm asking you about the external finding. Is it true that by way of external findings, external examination, you cannot establish what you've just referred to, the remaining quantity of blood in the organism? Am I right?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the basis of my knowledge and skill, I am able to assess, to estimate on the basis of the livores mortis and the flow rate, outflow rate of the blood from the cadaver, and other signs, I can tell whether the cadaver is completely devoid of blood or not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ciganovic, Dr. Ciganovic, I have to interrupt you. We are elaborating too much. Because I can directly ask you how do you know how much blood has flown out of a body from the place where the injury was sustained to the place of transportation to the hospital, et cetera, is it true that you cannot ascertain that?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the average, all people have about five litres of blood in their organism. I can ascertain the remaining quantity in the body.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I agree with that, but what remains in the body is something that you cannot ascertain by an external examination, and under external examination, I mean that there is no partial work, there is no entering into the body of any kind. Is that not so? Because -- because in that case, it would be called an internal examination, an internal finding when you actually access the internal parts of the abdominal cavity with your hands and with your instruments.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In forensic medical practice and in contacts with the investigating magistrate, once an external examination is ordered, a partial autopsy is taken -- undertaken as well, and other manipulation and procedures as well, so that when such a determination as to the examination of the corpse is issued, the judge either orders an external examination or an autopsy. There are no orders for a partial autopsy or anything else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So no court order on a partial autopsy exists.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I have never come across one -- such order in my practice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For any order on an external examination or a complete autopsy, are you under the obligation to prepare a report?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you have to incorporate in this report everything that you did and everything that you found? Just briefly yes or no.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree with the attitude with the -- of Professor Samuilo Pejakovic who says that concluding as to the finding -- as to the cause of death only on the basis of an external finding or external examination of a cadaver constitutes elemental ignorance on the part of whoever seeks to establish it in this way?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm always talking in forensic medical terms, about the external examination procedure only.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it also elementary ignorance -- is it -- when someone who derives conclusions as to the cause of death only on the basis of an external examination without any reservation at all?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you heard about the desecration of cadavers?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is it?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is unnecessary and illogical mutilation and damage by mutilation of a cadaver for motives which are not associated with any expedient aim, are not the subject, in other words, of medical manipulation or funeral rites.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true that a forensic medicine specialist may not give a conclusion on -- as to the cause of death only on the basis of an external examination of the cadaver?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then there is exhumation; right?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what the most frequent reason -- of course always talking about standpoint of the court and forensic medical business, what is the most frequent reason for an exhumation to be ordered by the decision of a court?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The decision of a judge.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I agree. Why?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The reasons can differ.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's what I ask.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a rule, it is because of the request of the relatives, next of kin of the deceased, because of the various doubts that they are raising and suspicions and similar. In my practice, the most frequent reason was the request of the next of kin.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true that there exist causes of deaths which have nothing to do with a visible injury?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, your wartime duty station was inscribed in your service booklet. Is it right?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, as did everybody else. All men who had done military service.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where exactly was your wartime duty station?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My station in wartime was in the civilian service in the Dubrovnik hospital.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you as a military conscript actually filled the vacancy in the civilian service?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, as a part of the civilian defence, the civilian protection. I was assigned to do my own job which I normally did otherwise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As a person subject to military service and in view of your fitness, could you have served in the field in any unit?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could have served in a unit in the field as far as my fitness was concerned and my health was concerned, but according to this assignment which I received from the then-military district, I was assigned to this post.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So this is the -- your duty station as a military conscript, as a person liable to military duty?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose so.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, shall it be a full hour and a half, Your Honour? Of course, taking --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I thought you were about to say you had concluded, Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, yeah, for the first session I have concluded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: For the first session. Well, we will adjourn now and have a 20-minute break. That's not to indicate we would be content with a full further session, Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Can I please have the usher's assistance, reports on external examination, P70, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ciganovic, is it true that the title of this document is Report on the External Examination of Dead Bodies, dated the 7th of December, 1991?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This document was compiled on behalf of the investigating judge of the district court in Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This document was compiled pursuant to an order of the Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Croatia, 511-01-55, dated the 6th of August, 1991; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what this order means? What this order is about, what it says, which tasks it envisages to be carried out?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with this order of the Ministry of the Interior that you have just cited. However, the entire procedure was quite common. It was the same procedure that was applied in peacetime conditions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So why is there this association that this report was drafted pursuant to that order?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not for me to say. This is something that the judge himself decides.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It is noteworthy that the commander of the identification platoon of the Dubrovnik Civilian Protection also attends this examination, Dr. Stipo Raguz. Is that his wartime assignment?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's his wartime assignment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: According to this report, this entire work was done between 0915 and 1300 hours; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is indeed what it says.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But is it correct? Can you remember that?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember specifically. I know that it was carried out in the morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: First of all, the crime technician placed marks - we saw those boxes with numbers - placed marks on the bodies, and the bodies were photographed, then the bodies were identified, which entailed an examination of their clothing and looking for documents, for personal documents. And if we look at the report, we see that witnesses were used to identify bodies. It was only then that the bodies were handed over to the autopsy-ist for examination.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct that each individual body was examined in this way, was processed in this way?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With external examinations being performed of the bodies, the examinations that you performed, everything was done within these three hours and 45 minutes?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you perform partial internal examination on all these 19 bodies, as you have stated?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only on those bodies where the injuries were so small that one couldn't look inside through the opening and see what sort of damage had been caused inside the body.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we conclude that on the basis of this report?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, mainly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we look at these 19 cases, can you specify those where you performed partial internal examinations? Can we see that if we look at this report?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since I read the reports in relation to these two cases, the case Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. of Pavo Urban and the case of the man named Skocko, I performed partial autopsy in these two cases because the injuries were small in terms of their size on the surface of the body. Therefore, it was necessary to make the opening, the entry wound, wider in order to get inside the body and see what occurred inside the body.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you perform partial autopsies on any other bodies in addition to the two that you've just referred to?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I should go through the report in order to be able to tell you that and then I can tell you. This was the case with Koviljka Kosjerina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please give me the number?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't necessary to carry out the partial autopsy. That's number one. Niko Mihocevic, number 2, no partial autopsy. Number 3, no partial autopsy. Number 4, none. Number 5, there was a partial autopsy. Number 6, none. Number 7, there was one. Number 8, none. Number 9, none. Number 10, none. Number 11, yes, there was one carried out. Number 12, yes, there was one. Number 13, none. Number 14, there was one. Number 15, there was one. Number 16, there was one. Number 17, none. Number 18, none. Number 19, yes, there was one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Therefore, having counted all these, in your opinion, eight bodies required partial autopsy, as you referred to it, which means part of the internal finding.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it not true that even in those eight cases you did not perform full autopsy?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it not true that in none of the eight cases did you actually specify that a partial autopsy had been carried out?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you determine the time of death for these bodies?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only in very rough terms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Based on the rigor mortis, based on where the livores mortis were apparent, I would estimate whether death occurred days ago or hours ago, and my conclusion in this specific case was that they had died the previous day. So about 24 hours earlier, approximately.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So in all these cases, the time of death was determined approximately as having occurred about 24 hours earlier?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, roughly speaking.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it not true that this report does not indicate the time of death for each individual body in terms of giving the exact time?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me if there is a difference between an explosive wound and a wound inflicted by a fragmentation projectile?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They both belong to the same category.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There's an explosion, detonation, there's an amount of pressure involved. Can this cause injury to a body, the so-called blast effect?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Blast effect occurs when there's a powerful explosion in the immediate vicinity of the body, especially in closed spaces, usually indoors. If, for example, a person is staying indoors in the house. Out of doors when there are explosions that are not that powerful, minor explosions, the consequences of the blast effect are usually not apparent.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we could put this more graphically, please, it doesn't matter whether the explosion is greater or smaller. An explosive wound, can there be an injury to the body just because an explosion occurs nearby without the projectile actually hitting the body? Can this be the case?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is possible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Also, but there's a difference there, an injury can be caused by a projectile or a fragment of a fragmentation projectile.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but these injuries are different.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it not true that in your findings no such difference is apparent; rather, all the conclusions indicate multiple explosive injuries for most of the bodies examined. Explosive wounds or multiple explosive injury; is that not true?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is true. What I had in mind were injuries caused by fragmentation projectiles.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But that's not what you wrote down, is it?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is the implication, because that's what an explosive injury implies. What you asked about is injury caused by detonation without the body being hit by shrapnel or fragments of a projectile. That's the blast-effect injury. The injury is usually to the intestines, to the lungs, to the eardrum, to the ear, and the like, and they're not even similar to these other injuries.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could those also be termed explosive injuries?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In forensic terms, these are not referred to as explosive injuries. These are referred to as blast injuries or blast-effect injuries.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we therefore agree that an explosive injury cannot cause death?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the cause of death is given, indicated clearly for each of these bodies. As far as I have been able to tell, in most cases it was haemorrhage, death caused by haemorrhage, and in some cases there was serious damage to vital organs, such as the brain.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ciganovic, I'm merely reading the transcript and I'm asking you questions in relation to what was stated in the transcript. And what the transcript reflects is as follows: Explosive injury, such as, for example, number 10.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can I ask where you're reading from?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm reading from the transcripts -- rather, from the report, number 10, P70.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Number 10, the last sentence reads: "The cause of death, multiple explosive injuries." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question is: Can an explosive injury cause death?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I do not agree with you. It can be the mechanism of inflicting an injury but not the cause of death itself. Is that not true?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In forensic medicine, a death-causing injury is directly related to a death that has occurred and is usually specified as the cause of death. These are such cases as drowning, shooting wounds, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ciganovic, this is not even logical what you're suggesting, because awhile ago in answer to one of the previous questions in connection with the cause of death, you said that if injuries caused to vital organs, that, too, can cause death, but this is not the same as explosive injury. You said yourself, after all, that there's a difference between the mechanism whereby an injury is brought about and the cause of death. These two are to be distinguished; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If multiple explosive injury is given as the cause of death, then there's no distinction between the cause of death and the mechanism whereby death occurs.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're a forensic medical expert; you know what that implies.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In all the cases where the cause of death was given as multiple explosive injury or just explosive injury, death was nearly instantaneous following fatal damage to vital organs in the body.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It is precisely in these conclusions from the report that we cannot seem to find a single reference to the vital organs and how death occurred. There is no distinction here.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Damage was described before the cause of death was given where death was not instantaneous but, rather, some time elapsed. It reads that the cause of death is an explosive injury with bleeding, with haemorrhage.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If, for example, we have an explosive injury to the right lower leg, is that the cause of death or is this the tool used to cause an injury?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: An explosive injury with all its consequences is the cause of death.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ciganovic, my question is very specific. An explosive injury to the right lower leg, is it only the tool whereby an injury is caused?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The tool used to cause an injury means establishing what the tool used was, in which direction the tool was used, how the tool operated, what the energy of the tool was. That's what we mean when we say "tool," a mechanism. The conclusion one may reach in these cases is that an explosive injury or a shooting wound can be the cause of death. And in medical doctrine, this is always given as the cause of death.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My submission to you, Mr. Ciganovic, is this is simply not true, because this can only be the mechanism of an injury. But the cause of death as a result of such an injury is the fact that one of the vital organs ceases to function.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is always the cause of death, one of the vital organs ceases to function. That's what we mean by clinical death.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The body contains quite a number of these vital organs, doesn't it, that can, in case of malfunction, cause death? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In relation to these 19 bodies that were examined, is it not true that this report does not specify as the cause of death the cessation of function of any vital organs?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You told us today that you don't even need to look at the report and that you still remember the work you performed on the body of the deceased, the late Pavo Urban; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also said that details of the autopsy performed on his body were extensively described in this report dated the 7th of December, 1991, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say that the details of the autopsy were described. The autopsy, the procedure itself was described in the same way as for all the other bodies. It's a very brief description, containing only the basic data that were established.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am quite certain that you were speaking about autopsies, but I think you were led to use the word by my learned friend and colleague, Mr. Re, because he kept asking about autopsies, so you used the term. But I'm certain you used the term on a number of occasions during your examination-in-chief. Tell me, then, sir, why is it that this report does not indicate in any way that partial internal examinations were carried out, that a partial internal examination was performed on the body of Pavo Urban?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Partial internal examinations of the bodies of all the persons that I have indicated was performed -- were performed, and in addition to that, full external examinations, head to toe, with all the symptoms, all the personal marks and all the other relevant marks that can be ascertained in this way, but this is not something that I recorded in this report. This report only reflects the most essential facts, and the reason is that the report was compiled under extraordinary circumstances while there was a lull in the shelling.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we agree that for a forensic report drawn up by a forensic medicine specialist, it is essential whether we have an external -- whether it is an external examination or an autopsy, it is essential that he indicate all the procedures undertaken and everything that was found both by the external and the internal examination; right?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In peacetime conditions, a post-mortem examination is undertaken in keeping with the regulations governing forensic medicine autopsies and involves an examination, external and internal examination, of the bodies, after which a report is made which indicates all the details of the findings after such examination and gives a final conclusion. In so doing, descriptions are given of different organs and parts of the body which are not significant in terms of the cause of death but are just normal and healthy parts of the body, because this is the way to show that all of these procedures were undertaken lege artis. In the event of extraordinary situations, we do not follow this procedure but, rather, we only describe the pathological signs and other elements which are of significance for the final finding.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I beg to differ, and that is because also when the circumstances are extraordinary, in a state of war, for instance in 1991, if you undertook what is indicated in the reports, which is external examinations of a dead body, and then for 19 persons you have an individual indication in -- before every single body to the effect that an external examination was undertaken, so that if you undertook partial internal examination of all these individual bodies, you had to record that particular operation also in your report because extraordinary circumstances are wholly immaterial in respect of that particular fact given everything which you have recorded in your report. Am I not right?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as I said, the court order can instruct one to just undertake an external examination or an autopsy. There does not exist the concept of a partial -- of partial autopsy. This is something that we forensic medical specialists undertake on our own in order to ascertain the truth. In respect of the court, it is still recorded as an external examination.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ciganovic, somebody may ask you in court, "How did you actually ascertain the serial number 9 where you indicated that a partial examination of the internal organs was required?" What answer will you give to prove that you did indeed undertake such a procedure when nothing is recorded there?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Under number 9, I don't think I indicated that number as a number in respect of which I undertook a partial autopsy, because this was a severe, extensive explosive wound, 20 centimetres in diameter with all the internal abdominal organs falling out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ciganovic, as you gave me these suggestions where you worked in detail, I jotted it down, and I jotted this down right next to serial number 9, but no problem. We can move on to another number. For instance, number 14. Here you also indicated that you were supposed to undertake a partial autopsy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. My note is obviously different to my learned friend's note. My note says that the witness said that he did not perform a partial autopsy on number 9.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: My note was numbers 5, 7, 11, et cetera, not number 9, Mr. Rodic. I must agree with Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: But you were moving on anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, well, I have eight or nine numbers marked.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us take, for instance, number 11.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You marked this as a body where you were to undertake a partial Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. internal analysis.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Number 11.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is there a single reference to such a procedure on your part in this finding relevant to number 11? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is the situation the same in respect of all these eight or nine marked numbers?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that even after certain years you are able to recall details in regard to your work on the body of the deceased Pavo Urban. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, for the most part.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In response to questions put to you by my learned colleague, you said that while working on the body of the late Pavo Urban, you found a fragment of an explosive shell inside the abdominal cavity near the spine.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You remember that today?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember everything which was connected to this particular deceased person.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In view of the fact that you say that the procedure required in respect of Pavo Urban for you to also undertake this internal examination because you found this part, this fragment of an explosive device, and now you remember today that you did indeed find that fragment.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you please take a look at serial number 15. So the medical part of the finding, the last paragraph. Can you tell me, please, where in this report is it indicated -- is the fact indicated that you found a fragment of an explosive device in the abdomen near the spine? Is it written in this report at all?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it is not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why is it not written, Mr. Ciganovic? Perhaps because you didn't find it, in fact.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It is not indicated in the other reports either. But this fragment of an explosive device could not have disappeared because the channel ended in the body. Where there were gunshot wounds, I didn't find explosive devices, but where you only have an entry wound without an exit wound, I always found the fragment of the explosive device in question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Ciganovic, as to the details, I do not wish to discuss those on the basis of this type of finding, but I do wish to stress that it is certainly the obligation of an expert, of a court autopsy-ist, if he finds an extraneous body in the corpse, to so specify in his finding. Is it not his obligation?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was noted by the diagnosis. Had I not found this device, I could have assumed what the cause of the explosive wound had been. It could have been a dynamite explosion in a mine or in a stone quarry with pieces of stone, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ciganovic, awhile ago in response to this question, you completely ruled out any dynamite explosions and similar explosions. So I submit to you that you are not saying the truth, and I will tell you why. Because you say that you didn't indicate this in any of the reports.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose I didn't. I haven't read all the reports in detail now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But can you follow one procedure in respect of some of these 19 bodies and then another procedure in respect of some of the other bodies?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, maybe it is possible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What does that depend on?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it depends on the time available for me to draw up these reports.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What prevented you?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was very cold. When we worked there was no electric power. We used lamps, torches, or during the day, in daylight, and we had no water. And we also had to work when there was a lull in the shelling. We were not aware of when the alarm would be sounded again, so that we had to go quickly about our work in order to finish it properly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ciganovic, as far as I know, you did this work on the 7th of December from 0915 hours to 1300 hours, and that was not in conditions of shelling, at least not on that day. Am I not right?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not remember that.
