utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My submission awhile ago to the effect that you were not saying the truth is based, for instance, on item 5. Please take a look at item 5. I shall read it out: "The following bodily wounds were established: On the anterior of the upper part of the right humerus, explosive wound of an irregular shape, contused and lacerated edges, diameter about 3 centimetres with a channel which goes backwards and leftwards and moves towards the inside part of the bone, ending just beneath the surface of the skin on the posterior side of the humerus where there is a small piece of shrapnel." I suppose, since this description has been given, that one could also palpate it. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you indicate -- in this particular report you indicate shrapnel but not in the case of Pavo Urban.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is about --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not asking you what this is about. I'm asking you whether this is a piece of shrapnel that belongs to the organism or is it an extraneous body?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an extraneous body.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Rodic, would you allow the witness to answer the question he is answering. You were interrupted, Doctor. Would you like to answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In case number 5, this was a minor bodily injury to the humerus with a relatively small wound channel, so it was necessary to establish why the victim had bled to death given that this was a wound to the soft tissues of the arm and what had been the cause of it. That is why this wound was opened, was processed, and we established the damage -- damage to have occurred to the main artery of the upper arm, and we found at the end of the channel a small piece of shrapnel which is a relatively small extraneous body which actually did lead to this type of injury. That is why it is specified here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Rodic, carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ciganovic, in -- is it prescribed for specialists of your profession what particular sizes of projectiles you are to indicate in your report and what sizes you are not to indicate? So the foreign bodies found, is there a classification by size of foreign bodies found in a body in terms of which are to be recorded in the report and which are not to be recorded in the report? Yes or no, please.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot give you a yes or no answer to that question, namely for the needs of the court or the investigation procedure, at times sometimes it is necessary to ascertain the type of extraneous body and sometimes it is not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I submit it to you, Mr. Ciganovic, that when you undertake that procedure for the court, you have to specify and establish in your findings all extraneous bodies that you find. This is what I submit to you.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do note I found a foreign body in the normal autopsy report, but as I said before, these were not the usual peacetime conditions of work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the body under serial number 5 and the body of Pavo Urban processed under the same conditions?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know who inserted this correction? It's in the report.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I assume it was the recording clerk.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which correction do you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's only one here in the report added. There is a bit of handwriting here. It relates to Pavo Urban.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who said that this correction should be inserted?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It could only have been you, the way I see it, because the recording clerk did not actually attend the autopsy itself.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's quite true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which means that you read this finding, and you must have spotted the mistake, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume I did, but I can't remember now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In addition to this single mistake, you made no other corrections and no other additions, did you?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not as far as I remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what we have to rely upon 13 years on is your recollection, your recollection that you found this piece of shrapnel, but it's not actually recorded in the report.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you told by anyone ever that perhaps you should paper over the shortcomings of this report using your story about partial work being carried out on the injuries, partial examinations of injuries?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you perhaps decide to do that of your own accord?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I always do the same thing. I always follow the same procedure in order to locate all the possible consequences of a bodily injury in order to get at the cause of injury or death.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We have agreed already, haven't we, that the tool used to cause death and the cause of death are two different things, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In forensic medicine, there's a link between these two and the immediate cause of death, and that's what you use to diagnose, to describe, as I've explained already.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, but there may be a distinction drawn between the mechanism on the one hand and the cause on the other, precisely because this mechanism in certain cases is not necessarily the cause of death at the same time. Isn't that the case?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If, for example, there is an entry and exit wound to the heart, you can't state that as the cause of the heart's death, but if you indicate that in the report just by itself without adding anything else, then the cause of death is crystal clear. This is the sort of terminology that is usually employed in forensic medicine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ciganovic, there are a number of us here who have worked for different courts, and we've had similar experiences. So please let us try to simplify. As you've said you testified many times --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Learned counsel from the Defence appears to be making a speech and attempting to turn it into a question at the end, I anticipate, by saying "am I right" or "do you agree with this?" It's not a proper way of asking questions and I object to this particular form of questioning. It's more of a comment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think there is some substance in what is put, Mr. Rodic. At this point you are getting really to putting some extensive propositions to the witness as assertions and then adding at the end, "Is this correct," or "Is this so?" Would you be able to be more careful in framing a question?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll do my best, Your Honour. Thank you very much for your assistance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So in reference to what we talked about, Mr. Ciganovic, if someone is injured in a traffic accident, for example, the leg is broken, after a month this person may die of pneumonia. Is that not possible?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is indeed a possibility.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that not imply there must be a distinction between, on the one hand, the mechanism whereby an injury comes about and the cause of death? These two are different things, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've encountered such cases in my career, and being an expert, I decided that there must be a distinction between the way an injury came about and the cause of death.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you were to write a report, what would you give as the cause of death in this particular case: The person was knocked down by a car and a leg was broken. Would that be indicated as the cause of death?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In such a case you would form a conclusion and include this conclusion in a section of the report that is usually entitled "The Expert's Opinion," and that's where I express my view of the causal link which caused death. But in the descriptive part, you give the diagnosis, you determine all the pathological changes that came about as a result of the wounding as well as any other changes that the body had been subjected to before that were not necessarily related to the cause of death.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In this specific example that I have given you, the cause of death, the immediate cause of death, the heart stopped pounding, for example, what would that be? Pneumonia, for example, or another lung disease, would that be the cause of death in that specific case?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, sir, did you know the investigating judge, Dragan Gajic, during your time in Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know Bruno Karmincic, who was the chief investigator for the district court in Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In early October 1991, did you perhaps perform an autopsy on the commander of Dubrovnik's civilian protection?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the man's name?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I forgot. I think the name was Valjalo or something like that but I can't recall the name. Bartos.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Bratos?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I remember now that you've said it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you perhaps remember anything in relation to that man? Did he go for negotiations with the JNA? Did he call on the people of Dubrovnik to remain calm and composed?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he perhaps call on the JNA to disarm paramilitary units?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The wording was not the same, but I did have occasion to listen to the announcement that he made over Radio Dubrovnik, where he announced that probably the next day, but I can't remember which day it was specifically, the JNA would enter Dubrovnik. He called on everyone to remain calm, to not cause trouble, and if they were in possession of any weapons, to hand those over to the soldiers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he not killed just after that, killed by his own car at the Pile Gate?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He drove in a white Zastava car, and he was killed from nearby, and you performed the autopsy, did you not?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure exactly how the whole thing began. I know that the report of the investigating judge stated that he was killed in the car from close range.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any JNA members in Dubrovnik at the time?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the summer of 1991, were there any incidents, houses being blown up, houses belonging to people who were ethnic Serbs living in the Dubrovnik area?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, cars were being blown up, cars belonging to such people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was anyone prosecuted or brought to account for these acts that were committed?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not to my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that during the war in Dubrovnik in October, November, and December 1991, you lived in three different places.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: First there was the house on JNA road, and from there you moved to Lapad. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please then tell me why at one point it became dangerous to stay at the house where you were staying?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because many shells were landing nearby around the house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you decided to move to Lapad, to stay there with friends, I assume.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You had heard that things were more peaceful in Lapad at the time?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely. Besides, my friends own a house which has a shelter in the basement while my own house was made of wood, and it was very old. Any direct impacts would have been fatal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But as time went by, the intensity of the shelling increased and it became dangerous to stay in Lapad as well, so you went back to the old town.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The shelling intensified in the Lapad area, and that place was even further off from where I worked. And I normally walked to work. There was a great deal of risk involved in crossing the area on foot several times a day under those circumstances.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, sir, throughout this period of time, October, November, December 1991, did you ever see Croatian soldiers in the town of Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the same period, did you ever see Croatian soldiers firing from inside Dubrovnik, firing at JNA positions?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't myself witness anything like that, but I did hear shells being fired.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In relation to what you heard, shells being fired, mortar shells being fired, are you familiar with such military positions as Bogisicev Park, Gradac Park --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... you've introduced mortar shells. I think you better clarify with the witness whether that is what he meant by "shells" before you put your question. He said "shells," not "mortar shells."

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours, but in the Serbian language I heard that the witness originally referred to mortar shells. So we can make a correction there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that correct, sir, you heard mortar shells being fired from the Croatian side?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The difference appears to be one of translation. Thank you, Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Ciganovic, I didn't hear you. We interrupted you. I was referring to those positions. Were you familiar with those positions, Bogisicev Park, Gradac Park, Lapad Park, Croatian mortars firing from those positions?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't personally see any mortars positioned there. The people did talk about these positions. I'm not sure if the stories I heard were accurate or not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You used to walk to work. Did you pass the Gradac Park on your way to work?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I walk right by it but not through the park itself, nor did I ever pass through the Bogisicev Park on my way to work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you said about personally hearing sounds of mortar shells being fired, which position was that a reference to?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's very difficult to specify the position.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just roughly speaking, which part of town was it?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were very few weapons around, very few mortars, judging by the sound. I heard them in different parts of town, some in Lapad and then the section between Lapad and the Old Town, and there were sounds coming from the Old Town also, but I couldn't tell exactly where the sounds were coming from.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about when you heard these sounds of firing coming from the Old Town? Was that when you went to the Old Town to stay there, as you said?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Maybe it's the translation again, but the transcript says there were sounds coming from the Old Town. The witness said didn't say, according to the English translation, sounds of firing coming from the Old Town.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour. Your Honour, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: If you would like to clarify that with the witness, Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were listing -- you were listing the different places from which you heard sounds of firing from a mortar. Lapad, the section between Lapad and the Old Town, and you said in the Old Town itself, but you couldn't tell from where exactly. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is true that I heard sounds of firing while I was in all those places, but I must clarify the following: Dubrovnik is a very small town. Between these detonations, there was absolute still, and in those periods of silence, you could hear sounds like that from a great distance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Fair enough. My question was about the times you heard firing from the Old Town. Was that in the same period of time when you lived in that flat behind the cathedral in the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was in that period of time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, sir --

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I please have Mr. Usher's assistance. I would like to show the witness this photograph.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ciganovic, in the period of 1991 under discussion, while you moved about town, did you ever see this three-barrel weapon mounted on a truck in the town of Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I personally never saw this weapon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear about this weapon and -- did you hear about this weapon moving about town?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did hear about the existence of this weapon and about the weapon moving about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear that there were two or three other such trucks in addition to this three-barrel weapon, with mortars mounted even?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard about a truck with a mortar mounted on it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you perhaps hear about these weapons being used for firing or, rather, excuse me, these weapons were firing from those trucks and they were moving quickly from place to place.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see any such thing myself, but I assume that this was the case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You assume that they were moving about and firing?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I please ask Mr. Usher to show the next photograph to the witness. And, Your Honours, if this photograph can please be received into evidence and be assigned a Defence exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The first photo will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Defence Exhibit D35.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ciganovic, you can see the writing on the truck, "Kobra." Have you ever seen that before or heard about it?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you ever heard about a Croatian unit that was called the same?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can no longer remember now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. In view of the places where you resided throughout the period and you moving about town, did you perhaps hear that a small lorry like that was positioned at Lihtenstajnov Put, which is at a distance of about 80 metres from the Libertas Hotel?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I heard nothing about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, did you know about any positions of the Croatian army in Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in that period, because whenever I moved about, there was no shelling from any side, so wherever I went, I never saw any weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, do you know if there were any clashes in Dubrovnik between the HOS extremists and the members of the National Guard?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't speak about that. I'm not familiar with that. I did not have an opportunity to familiarise myself with anything like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you ever called to the Dubrovnik Crisis Staff headquarters?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not as far as I remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have any communication with anyone from the Dubrovnik Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With some of the officials, yes, when they issued us with a permit to leave Dubrovnik during a cease-fire. I left Dubrovnik to go and visit my family.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please describe exactly what happened? It was during a cease-fire, and you were issued a permit. What exactly did that mean?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I obtained this permit to leave town for several days to be able to go and visit my family. My family were then staying in Sarajevo, and I got in touch with someone, I'm not sure what the person's official position was or the importance of that person, but that person issued me with a permit, a pass.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true that without that pass, that permit, you would not have been allowed to leave Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's quite true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was in charge of issuing such permits? It was the Dubrovnik Crisis Staff, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I assume so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At that time in October, November, December 1991, did you see any armed people moving about Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did see members of the Croatian army who were uniformed and were carrying small arms, usually automatic rifles.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Infantry weapons.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, infantry weapons, but a very small number of soldiers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever see any civilians moving about armed, carrying infantry weapons, rifles, perhaps?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever see any armed soldiers inside the Old Town on your way home or on your way to work?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but very seldom. Mostly whenever I saw these soldiers, they were without weapons. I know that they had been forbidden to move about town in their own spare time armed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But there were occasions when you saw them with weapons, weren't there?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there different kinds of uniforms, of military uniforms?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so. The way I remember, they all looked the same to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you left Dubrovnik for Sarajevo, did you leave Dubrovnik by a vessel?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, through Mokosica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who, if anyone, controlled you on the way out?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume -- I assume it was a military checkpoint. I don't remember whose military checkpoint. On the one side I believe it was the Croatian army, and across the way it was the JNA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know where the Territorial Defence headquarters were?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember whether it was the Petka Hotel at Gruz. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you perhaps see anyone at the aquarium?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a civilian shelter there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any members of Territorial Defence there?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see any there. I went there several times myself during shelling, and everyone I met there were civilians.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, where did you have to go to get your permit from the Crisis Staff to leave town?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, I no longer remember where the Crisis Staff HQ was. I think it was at Gruz, at the Petka Hotel, but I can't be sure about this. I've forgotten.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where is the municipality building in Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The municipality building is in the same building as the municipal and district court. The municipal administration, where the mayor is, that's back in the Old Town, next to the rector's palace.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know where Vila Rasica is?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us where?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is between Gradac and Gruz.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know if perhaps the ZNG had their headquarters there?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I think I made a mistake. This villa is between Gradac and the Old Town. Yes. That used to be a students' home before, and I heard that they were there, Croatian soldiers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, sir, the Territorial Defence headquarters, was that across the way from the medical centre, from the health centre?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just across the way from the medical centre there's the old recruitment office building, but I'm not sure if that building had any specific use during the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know a man named Zeljko Pavlovic?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The name's not familiar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know where the Hotel Zagreb is?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. It is in the Lapad inlet.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the command of the defence of Dubrovnik there perhaps? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember. Possibly it was. I think that I heard it was there, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the Croatian Party of Rights -- did the Croatian Party of Rights had a unit called Sokol, "the falcon," in Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you familiar with Bozo Miljanic?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've heard of him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it not true that he was an extremist that blowed up Serbian houses in the territory of Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can recall, he was the president of the commission for the demolition of houses which had been built without authorisation, without a permit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do -- are you familiar with the zone of the city which is called the Chinese Wall?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see any military -- any Croatian troops there, military forces?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't pass through those parts of town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the mortar positions in the Montovjerna zone?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not. As I have said, I never saw any weaponry because during the shelling I would either be in a shelter -- for the most part I would be in a shelter, and when there was no shelter, I never came across any weapons.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: When there was no shelling, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, do you know where the old people's home in Dubrovnik is?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are two senior citizens' homes, one in the Old Town and one in the vicinity of the old hospital in Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you pass by that road, by either of these two old peoples' homes?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have occasion to see members of the National Guard Corps on those locations? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I saw some of them individually in the street, and where they were stationed or located, I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As regards members and the positions or operations of the Croatian army, you couldn't see any of those while you were in the shelter; right?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when this danger ceased, would those positions be changed? Would those people withdraw?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only assume, because I never saw any piece of heavy ordnance during that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown Defence Exhibit D28.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever have an opportunity to -- to see the mortar in Bogisicev Park open fire?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps if you take a look at the photograph you can have a better view. And can you recognise the person in the photograph?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please tell me, did you undertake examinations of the bodies of members of the Croatian army as well?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there quite a few of such examinations?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were quite a few of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did anyone indicate for you that these were members of the Croatian army or was it a conclusion that you derived for yourself?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would be given information to that effect from the investigating team which would come to the autopsy, which also happened in these instances, but these bodies would, as a rule, had been brought to me in uniforms and even with light armaments.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And would they tell you on such occasions at which positions these people had sustained their injuries or, rather, been killed, in which places?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, usually, not always but usually they would tell me where the person had been killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As you said that in October to December, you were the one who examined most of the bodies. I believe the figure you mentioned was above 100.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, above 100.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me, in addition to this report which we have here before us from the 7th of December, were these other examinations similar as this recorded in this report? Namely, were the reports of those examinations similar, indicating the same data as this one?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The examinations were similar. Some of them were different when there was a different cause of death because people also got killed in other ways, something which was not directly associated with the war, in other words.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So these deaths which were not directly caused by the war or associated with the war, were they caused by firearms?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there were some deaths by firearms, and people had also drowned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were some of these deaths -- do you know whether any of these cases were in fact -- do you know that any of the people who had caused the deaths of these people were tried by courts in Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose that they were, because the whole investigative procedure was actually conducted with this view in mind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were these people who were tried in Dubrovnik in the area of Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I believe that they were from the area of Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they accessible to the police bodies in the territory of the Dubrovnik municipality?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot respond to that question with certainty because I had no opportunity to familiarise myself with the facts of such cases.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were these people who stood trial for such acts, were they from the territory of Dubrovnik municipality? Were they residing in Dubrovnik municipality when these deaths occurred?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At that time, they certainly did reside in the territory of Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you at all remember whether anyone was -- inflicted the mortar wounds from firearms in terms of Croatian army members killing civilians or mutually killing each other?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were some sporadic instances of that type where both Croatian soldiers and policemen and civilians were killed. There was also one case of many people drowning when a ship sunk in the Gruz port and many people perished.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ciganovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, that completes my cross-examination. Can I please ask that this second photograph also be given a number as a Defence exhibit. These are all photographs from the exhibit of the Prosecution which our learned colleague Mr. Kaufman submitted to the Court yesterday. That is OTP Exhibit 66.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: These are from that video film, are they, Mr. Rodic?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: On that basis, this last photograph will be received as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Defence Exhibit D36.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will have a 20-minute break now.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Before Your Honours adjourn --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I was just noting the time the Court has fixed for the break and I anticipate maybe 15 minutes in re-examination. Do Your Honours wish to hear, start with the witness, that is Mr. Jovic, as late as half past six or would it be safe to send him home -- back to his hotel for the weekend?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: How long do you see your re-examination, Mr. Re?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Possibly 15 minutes or so, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think that would give us a useful time to commence with the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Re. Re-examined by Mr. Re:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Rodic, Dr. Ciganovic, asked you a number of questions about your reasons for leaving Dubrovnik at the end of December 1992, and you told the Trial Chamber that your wife and your five-year-old son had left to go to Pancevo. Did your wife and five-year-old son leave before or after the shelling of Dubrovnik had started?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: She left after the shelling, when women, children, and the elderly started leaving Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was it about the prevailing circumstances in Dubrovnik that led you to oppose your wife and five-year-old son's early return to Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I assumed that the war in Dubrovnik was not yet over by the end of 1991. My main concern was for their safety.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were also questioned about the need or otherwise for what the Defence were calling a full internal autopsy, and you gave some fairly extensive reasons for the circumstances in which you would perform a partial or an external examination. In coming to that -- sorry. In making that determination of whether to perform a partial internal examination, do you consider the history given to you in relation to the body being brought to the autopsy room? That is, the circumstances described as to why they were being brought there?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is one of the things I take into account, but that is not the only thing I take into account.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One of the things you were questioned about was a person being brought in after a traffic accident. In those sort of circumstances, that is, a traffic accident victim, what role does the history have in your determining whether or not to perform an internal autopsy?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If it is a pedestrian who was hurt in a traffic accident, it is necessary to take a blood sample to analyse it for alcohol. It's necessary to describe in detail all the external injuries in order to understand what sort of a traffic accident had occurred. It's necessary to carry out an internal examination in order to establish the cause of death. If the cause of death is obvious on external examination, then the judge usually orders only for an external examination of the body to be conducted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you consider the date or time of death given to you in the history - I'm only talking about traffic accidents at the moment - in determining whether or not to perform a partial or internal autopsy?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not if there is no significant aberration in terms of time, meaning not if the accident itself or death occurred on the previous day or even on the same day. Then this piece of information is not decisive.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll now take you to the same scenario but with explosive injuries. What significance does the history given to you in relation to the time and date of death have in your determining whether or not to perform a partial internal autopsy?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is the same as with explosive injuries. If death occurred on the previous day or on the same day, the exact time of the event itself is not material to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that differ with multiple bodies being brought in on the same day with a history of having been perhaps killed the day before?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In peacetime conditions, this would not be particularly important, and every body was processed as if it was the only body being brought in.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about in wartime?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In wartime, as was the case, in such conditions you only did what was absolutely necessary, so that even in situations where we had a smaller number of bodies, fewer bodies, or even just one body, only an external examination was done, accompanied, perhaps, by a partial autopsy to ascertain damage and the cause of death and any internal injuries.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the fact of there being multiple bodies brought in on one day affect or influence your decision to conduct a partial autopsy?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please now turn to your report, which is in front of you. It's MFI 70, and in each of the 19 bodies that you have identified as having examined, there are two paragraphs. The first starts with external examination, and the second paragraph refers to the details, what you actually did. Just for complete clarity of the meaning of "external examination," why does it only appear in the first paragraph of all the two paragraphs next to each of the 19 separate reports?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the first paragraph, there is data that was determined by the court, by the police, by the investigating bodies, the identity of the victim and the way in which the body was identified. In the second part is a description which I dictated. The first sentences of the description contain basic information on the body, which is mostly the same in all these cases, and this information indicates that these are relatively fresh bodies on the basis of the characteristics that these bodies -- of the features that these bodies display. And in the following paragraph you have the types of injuries sustained and the cause of death.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What I'm getting to, Doctor, is the meaning of the word "external" which appears only as the first word in each of the first paragraphs. Do we take it from what you just said it's a pro forma which refers to the visual identification or examination of a body when it first comes in?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is a pro forma. It is a juridical term. The court distinguishes between external examination and autopsy. The court determines that an external examination should be conducted and that's what was written down here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is there any other connection between the word "external" as it appears in the first paragraph of each of the two paragraphs and your findings in the second paragraph, or is it only related to the visible external examination of a body for identification when it arrives?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This does not refer to the external examination of the body immediately upon arrival. It refers to everything that has been noted down in reference to an individual.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Rodic also asked you about the difference between bodies showing sign of a blast effect and explosive injuries. Do any of the bodies, any of the 19 bodies upon which you -- which you examined on the 17th of December, 1991, show signs of a blast effect that you described?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I found no signs of a blast effect on any of these bodies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You gave evidence and were cross-examined about your examination or partial autopsy on the body of Mr. Pavo Urban, the photographer. What is it that causes you to remember this particular partial autopsy you performed on him?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This person was familiar to me from before, and his death caused a lot of commotion among friends, acquaintances, and his next of kin. His mother was there too. So that's why I remember this event in a particularly vivid way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were also questioned about firing that you heard when you were living in three different houses in Dubrovnik, and you said that you heard firing from the Old Town when you were living there. Were you inside a building or outside when you heard firing in the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sometimes I was outside the building when I heard sounds of firing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also said you occasionally saw some soldiers in the vicinity of the Old Town, mostly unarmed. What did the soldiers that you saw there appear to be doing?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My assumption was that they had been brought there to defend Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Rodic also cross-examined you about performing autopsies on military personnel. What was the most common cause of death you found in those autopsies?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Based on external examination and partial autopsy of all the bodies of dead soldiers that I inspected, in most of the cases it was the explosive injuries that had caused death.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember any autopsies on soldiers with gunshot wounds? And if so, would you be able to tell the Trial Chamber, estimate what percentage had gunshot wounds as opposed to explosive injuries?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were such cases, yes, but only a very small percentage. Not more than 5 per cent, or perhaps even less.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Could Your Honours just excuse me for one moment. I just need to consult with Ms. Somers, with your leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: That concludes my re-examination. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Doctor, in a number of the notes that were recorded in that report you prepared on the 7th of December, you have used the initials "OM" in your general description of the body. Can you tell the Chamber what that means.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is an abbreviation for the common medical term "osteomuscular," build, the build of a body.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Doctor, I'm pleased to be able to tell you that that brings to an end your evidence [yourself]. You are at last free to return. You are excused from further attendance, and thank you very much for your assistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The next witness, Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes, that's Mr. Nikola Jovic, who is outside one of the witness rooms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I see the transcript ascribes to me some amazing Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. powers. I am recorded as having told the doctor that he brought to an end himself rather than his evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good evening, Mr. Jovic. If you'd be good enough to take the affirmation. Read --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: If you'd like to sit down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Re. Examined by Mr. Re:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good evening, Mr. Jovic. Could you please give the Trial Chamber your full name.

utterances.speaker: Nikola Jovic
utterances.text: Nikola Jovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your occupation?

utterances.speaker: Nikola Jovic
utterances.text: I'm a merchant.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you live in -- a merchant. What do you actually do?

utterances.speaker: Nikola Jovic
utterances.text: I'm in charge of a supermarket and a manager.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that in the Old Town of Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: Nikola Jovic
utterances.text: Yes, in the Old Town of Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you live in Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: Nikola Jovic
utterances.text: Yes, I live in Dubrovnik in the Gruz area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long have you lived in Gruz area in Dubrovnik for?

utterances.speaker: Nikola Jovic
utterances.text: Since 1971.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how long have you worked in the supermarket in the Old Town of Dubrovnik for?

utterances.speaker: Nikola Jovic
utterances.text: Since 1990. Since April 1990.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you worked there continuously since April 1990?

utterances.speaker: Nikola Jovic
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you married?

utterances.speaker: Nikola Jovic
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you have any children who were born before the war?

utterances.speaker: Nikola Jovic
utterances.text: I have a daughter who turned -- who was one year, 11 months old during the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That means she was born in 1989; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Nikola Jovic
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were you born in 1963?

utterances.speaker: Nikola Jovic
utterances.text: That is correct, on the 15th of September.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, can you please tell the Trial Chamber about your JNA -- sorry, your JNA service.

utterances.speaker: Nikola Jovic
utterances.text: I served the JNA in 1982 and 1983, and I served in Kosovo in the towns of Pec and Prizren.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which department of the military did you work in?

utterances.speaker: Nikola Jovic
utterances.text: I was a Maljutka, which was a saljo [phoen] or anti-tank missile operator. It is a guided anti-tank missile.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What sort of experience or expertise did you gain in the use or operation of Maljutka missiles?

utterances.speaker: Nikola Jovic
utterances.text: While I did my military service, I was trained as a crew member to service these missiles.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you mobilised during the war in 1991?

utterances.speaker: Nikola Jovic
utterances.text: On the 26th and the 27th of September in 1991, I was summoned to respond to the call-up, but for the civilian defence, and I responded, and we were then located at the Hotel Stadion in Gruz. And then on the 1st of October, 1991, when the attack on Dubrovnik started, when the first shells landed on Komolac and the Mokosica, I was sent with another five men in a civilian van which was driven by one of our people. We were not in uniform. We were driven to the area of Orasac. In Orasac we were supposed to be provided with the Maljutka missiles in order to open fire at the two warships of the Yugoslav navy which were in the channel between Lopud and the place named Orasac. These vessels were opening fire at trucks, at means of transportation that were leaving Slano, and it was the only road which led to Dubrovnik, the only open road from Slano to Dubrovnik, because all other communication links had been severed, both air and road ones. There we were put up at the Vrtovi Sunca Hotel, and we spent there some two or three days. On the third day, they informed us that the then-JNA had entered Slano, so we withdrew with the civilians. Some of the civilians remained. Some of those who were fleeing from the surrounding places came to Vrtovi Sunca. Others remained. Some had their own boats, some had their relatives in Dubrovnik, some fled to the island of Lokrum, some to Lopud, but most of them remained there. So we withdrew and we went aboard an Atlas ship from Zaton to Babin Kuk. When I say "we," I mean a certain group of civilians, and this van which we used to transport ourselves remained in Zaton. And then we returned and on the 4th or the 5th I reported to the command. I cannot recall its precise name at this point, but that was already - how shall I put it? - at that time in Dubrovnik we already had widespread panic and anarchy because the army was advancing towards Zupa and Osojnik, and since we did not get this -- these weapons, the Maljutkas, they sent me home. I stayed at home for several days. They didn't call me, and then I started to work. So all this time that I spent in the army with my stay in Orasac and at the Stadion Hotel, this all lasted for six or seven days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who issued the call-up papers to you?

utterances.speaker: Nikola Jovic
utterances.text: The postman.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you saying they came in the post?

utterances.speaker: Nikola Jovic
utterances.text: No. The mailman would personally come to serve such papers on one. And they brought them to your home address. They, too, had probably been mobilised.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm asking you do you know which authority issued the papers to you through the post?

utterances.speaker: Nikola Jovic
utterances.text: I believe that by that time had already been organised the civilian defence or whatever its name was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said you went to Orasac. How far is that from Dubrovnik and in which direction?

utterances.speaker: Nikola Jovic
utterances.text: That is in the -- it is west -- to the west of Dubrovnik, north-west of Dubrovnik. It is some 20 kilometres away from Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were given no weapons and no uniform. Were you given a rank in that week you were with the military?

utterances.speaker: Nikola Jovic
utterances.text: No, I wasn't. I was in my normal civilian clothes, and not only I but all the rest of us, all the six of us, we were not issued with any weapons. We were supposed to be issued with these Maljutkas. Why we didn't get any, I couldn't say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you provided with any training in those six or seven days?

utterances.speaker: Nikola Jovic
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said you then went back home. Did you go back to work in your shop?

utterances.speaker: Nikola Jovic
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you ever called up again after that?

utterances.speaker: Nikola Jovic
utterances.text: Not until the 31st of December.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Between when you went home in your civilian clothes and the 31st of December, were you a member of the military or a civilian?

utterances.speaker: Nikola Jovic
utterances.text: I was a civilian. In fact, during these six or seven days which I spent with the army, this was not recorded anywhere. So I was also a civilian then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever receive any pay from the military for your six or seven days at Orasac?

utterances.speaker: Nikola Jovic
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about these JNA ships? Where were they?

utterances.speaker: Nikola Jovic
utterances.text: Well, there were two vessels which cruised alternately from Mljet -- from Mljet, the island of Mljet to the island of Lopud. So they were some way down in the middle of the channel.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were they doing when they were cruising alternatively between Lapad and --

utterances.speaker: Nikola Jovic
utterances.text: Lopud. They were opening fire at lorries, at least while we were in Orasac. A truck was hit in Trsteno and the driver of the truck suffered a light injury. It was a Dalmacijavino truck which was transporting wine to the Dubravkina shops in Dubrovnik. And there were other trucks that had been hit because they probably thought that these trucks were transporting weapons, but not only weapons because they wouldn't let any provisions be taken into the city, any supplies for the citizens.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Apart from lorries, were any buildings hit by firing from the JNA ships?

utterances.speaker: Nikola Jovic
utterances.text: I don't know whether any buildings were hit during that time when we were in Orasac, because they withdrew on that day, on the 3rd or the 4th when Slano had fallen. They were not in the channel any longer, and there was no need for them to be after the road had been blockaded.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Between September, October, November, and up to the 6th of December, 1991, did you see from Dubrovnik or anywhere else JNA warships firing on any targets in Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: Nikola Jovic
utterances.text: Yes. They called them gunboats. These were warships, and I could see them because I live in Gruz, in a section called Sipsino, and from there one has a good view of Lapad and Babin Kuk and the open sea towards the island of Daksa, and generally the sea, so at the end of October or the beginning of November, those ships stay there for some four or five or six days, constantly attacking Dubrovnik as -- and also fire was opened from surrounding positions from gunboats. And I could see that from my flat in which I still live today, because they were opening fire at hotels, at private houses where there were people. There were refugees in those hotels. They opened random fire at Lapad and Babin Kuk.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were any buildings damaged from this -- from these attacks?

utterances.speaker: Nikola Jovic
utterances.text: Yes, quite a few private houses were damaged, and I also believe that several civilians were killed in Babin Kuk in their houses. The Hotel Kompas was hit, the Hotel Park, the Hotel Palace, and a number of other hotels were hit as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've described firing from the sea. Were there any other -- did you know of any other JNA positions on land?

utterances.speaker: Nikola Jovic
utterances.text: Since I live in Sipsino, from there I could see all the way up to Petrovo Selo and Osojnik, and from that area they were also opening fire towards Gruz and the port of Gruz and at Lapad. The Gruz area where the Hotel Stadion is, where the bakery was. At that time, the old port in Gruz, there were several nice vessels, ships in the old part of Gruz. There was a very nice sailboat of the Atlas Travel Agency. There were other several ships that were burnt, and then there were some storehouses in the Gruz harbour which contained wood, timber, grain. And I remember when these went on fire that they actually illuminated the whole area so it seemed to be daylight in the middle of night. Then there was also another warehouse where coffee -- which was -- with coffee which was hit and the coffee burnt for several days and one could smell the aroma of coffee burning. At that time I was not working and at that time was one of the most vehement attacks on Dubrovnik. We were -- we didn't work for five or six days. We dare not move about. We went to fetch water at night because there was only water in the part of the city where the Buninovo cemetery is, and there is an old well which was dug by the Dubrovnik -- residents of Old Dubrovnik when there was no regular water supply in the city and this is the water well which was used by the civilians at that time. For bread we would also go to the bakery at night, and this bakery worked around the clock.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, just one part of the statement of the witness is not in the transcript. He said several days and the -- and the general alert which was on during the several days. So can that be put in its proper place in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Petrovic. Yes, Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Jovic, can you please listen carefully to the question. The question was related to JNA positions on land. Can you tell the Trial Chamber if you knew where the JNA -- if there were any JNA positions on land were. That's all.

utterances.speaker: Nikola Jovic
utterances.text: As for land positions around the city of Dubrovnik, there were positions at Osojnik, and everything had been occupied; Mokosica, Rozat, all the way up to Sustjepan, and then through Brgat and the Bosanka, the area of Srdj, all the way up to the Hotel Belvedere. This was all occupied and held by the then-JNA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were the Croat positions?

utterances.speaker: Nikola Jovic
utterances.text: The Croatian positions were down there in Kantafig, the Gruz area, Sustjepan, the fort on the hill of Srdj above Dubrovnik, and the Hotel Belvedere.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember any specific days in which there was shelling by the JNA of Dubrovnik and specifically the Old Town before the 6th of December?

utterances.speaker: Nikola Jovic
utterances.text: Before the 6th of December, if I remember correctly, two shells had landed in the Old Town in the early morning hours. I think it was the end of October, but I cannot recall the exact date. I only know that these two shells landed in the Old City before the 6th of December, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the consequence of the shells landing in the Old Town for the people in the Old Town? What happened as a result?

utterances.speaker: Nikola Jovic
utterances.text: You mean those two shells or you mean the 6th of December?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The two shells.

utterances.speaker: Nikola Jovic
utterances.text: Those two shells landed, and one of them hit a house on Miha Pracata Street, but I can't remember specifically, and the other hit the house next to this one. So I don't think there were any civilian casualties, but there was a lot of damage. One section of an entire wall had been demolished, a whole section of the street, but I don't think there were any civilian casualties then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was the -- what was the address of your shop?

utterances.speaker: Nikola Jovic
utterances.text: My shop is on Miha Pracata Street, number 11.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was your shop open for the entire period of October, November, and up to the 6th of December, 1991, or did it close at any time?

utterances.speaker: Nikola Jovic
utterances.text: Well, it remained closed only during the heavy shelling, as I described. It was in late October or early November. We stayed shut for those five days. There was the general alert and shells kept landing all over town, with the exception of the Old Town, at least in that period. I think there was a high number of civilian casualties in that period of time. That was the heaviest shelling. It was some of the most severe shelling. We weren't open in that period of time. We were back in Gruz, and the shop was in the Old Town. We couldn't go to work, and there was no way to get bread.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why do you say you don't think there were any civilian casualties when the two shells landed?

utterances.speaker: Nikola Jovic
utterances.text: Well, I think not. I didn't say that there weren't. I said that I didn't believe there were any.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Is this a convenient time with the witness, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I would expect so, Mr. Re, given your gentle indication. We will break now for the weekend, resuming Monday morning. Mr. Jovic, we've come to the end of our sitting day. I'm afraid I must ask you to come back on Monday morning.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that's fine, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I hope you enjoy The Hague. We will adjourn for the weekend.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Your Honour, before you leave, this doesn't concern this witness, it concerns the previous witness. When would be a convenient time? If there is still an objection to the tender of those documents, it will have to be addressed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Can we take that up at the end of the evidence for this witness, and unless it is going to produce a great difficulty, that would be a convenient time to deal with the outstanding legal submission which has kept Mr. Kaufman on hand. That's understood as well by Mr. Petrovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours, but the Defence wishes to point out that in relation to these documents referred to by Mr. Re, we have the objections from our cross-examination, but other than that, the Defence has no objection to these exhibits being received into evidence. As far as we're concerned, it can in fact be done right away, as concerns the exhibits in relation to the previous witness, Mr. Ciganovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think rather than delay everybody to go through them and identify them and have them recorded, we'll deal with that on Monday, but I'm very grateful for your indication, Mr. Petrovic. It seems we can deal with that fairly quickly on Monday.
